Thank you, Neelam John. Excellencies, distinguished guests, dear colleagues and friends, good afternoon. It's my great pleasure to welcome you to today's high level side event. I also warmly welcome representatives of member states, civil society organizations, colleagues, and friends of Afghanistan, and most importantly, Afghan women joining us from inside and outside Afghanistan. Your presence today sends an important message. The rights and future of Afghan women and girls must remain at the center of the international agenda on Afghanistan. Your presence today sends an important message. The rights and future of Afghan women and girls must remain at the center of international agenda on Afghanistan. Excellencies, five years into Taliban rule, the situation is no longer one of temporary restrictions or isolated decrees. What we are witnessing is the progressive institutionalization of systematic discrimination against women and girls. The latest report of the special rapporteur documents how these restrictions now affect almost every fundamental aspect of women's lives, education, employment, freedom of movement, access to public life, freedom of expression, and participation in decision making. The report further notes that these discriminatory measures have increasingly been codified, including through the 2024 law on the prevention of virtue and prevention of vice and subsequent decrees. The facts speaks clearly. Girls above sixth grade have remained excluded from secondary education since 2021. Women have been banned from universities since December 2022. And in December 2024, women were also prohibited from attending medical and health training institutions, cutting off the future supply of female nurses, midwives, and other health professionals, with serious consequences for Afghanistan's already struggling health sector. Women have also been systematically pushed out of employment. The ban on women's beauty salons alone reportedly affected approximately 12,000 businesses and cost some 60,000 women their jobs. Women civil servants were forced to remain at home, had their salaries reduced to only 5,000 Afghanis per month, regardless of their qualifications or experience. before their contracts were later terminated. The law on the elimination of violence against women was abolished. Specialized courts, prosecution offices, and police family response units were dismantled, and nearly all shelters protecting women and girls facing abuse have been closed. Approximately 250 women judges, around 10% of Afghanistan's judiciary, were removed from the bench. These are not simply statistics. Behind every number is a woman denied a profession, a girl denied a classroom, a family deprived of income, and a generation being denied of the opportunity to shape their own future. This brings us to the central question of today's discussion. What does accountability mean when violations are systematic and institutionalized and allowed to continue year after year? Accountability must certainly include legal mechanisms, documentation, preservation of evidence, and justice for victims. But it must mean more. It must mean that systematic discrimination carries consequences. It must mean that political engagement does not become political normalization. And it must mean that fundamental rights of Afghan women and girls are not treated as negotiable in exchange for access, stability, or short-term political convenience. At the same time, Afghan women must not be viewed only as victims. They are rights holders, political actors, experts, leaders, and essential stakeholders in Afghanistan's future. Their participation cannot be symbolic. It cannot be confined to separate consultations after decisions have already been made. Afghan women must be present where decisions about Afghanistan are discussed, negotiated, and made. Five years is long enough to know that waiting for these policies to change on their own is not a strategy. The international community needs a principled, coordinated, and sustained approach that places human rights, justice, accountability, and meaningful participation of Afghan women at the center of every engagement concerning Afghanistan. because there can be no legitimate, peaceful or sustainable future for Afghanistan while half of its population is systematically excluded from it. I conclude with that and I thank you.

Excellencies, distinguished panelists, ladies and gentlemen, welcome and thank you for joining us today. It has now been five years since women and girls in Afghanistan are systematically excluded from education, higher education, employment, freedom of movement, and many other basic and fundamental rights. Since returning to power, the Taliban have issued scores of decrees restricting the rights and freedom of women and girls in Afghanistan. Today, the situation of women in Afghanistan is not only a human rights crisis. It is a profound humanitarian, social, economic, institutional, and political crisis. And the consequences are felt across the country. According to UNICEF, Afghanistan is projected to lose approximately 25,000 female health workers by 2030, with insufficient human resources to fill the resulting gap. According to UNFPA, maternal mortality is more than 600 maternal deaths per 100,000 live births, resulting from preventable and treatable conditions. These figures are not simply statistics. Behind each number is a woman, a girl, a family, and a community whose future is being denied. And yet, over these five years, the international response has been limited to statements and characterized by hesitation, fragmentation, and so-called pragmatic approach that has involved incentives for the Taliban and exclusion of Afghanistan's women and democratic forces. Dear colleagues, we must be honest about the consequences. Engagement with no accountability has not produced any meaningful result. In fact, it has weakened the position of the international community, Afghan women, democratic forces, civil society, and even those elements of the Taliban who might be open for dialogue. Dear colleagues, the situation in Afghanistan also raises a question about global women's leadership and solidarity. When approximately 20 million women and girls are being systematically dehumanized, where is the collective response of the global women's movement? Where is the solidarity of human rights defenders to stand side by side with Afghan women and men who are demanding justice, inclusion, and rights for all? We are suppressed and isolated by the Taliban, but also abandoned by the world. While the world is still thinking and figuring out how to deal with the Taliban, Afghan women are organized. We have documented violations, supported survivors, delivered humanitarian assistance, and built network of solidarity. We have also led politically. We have engaged governments, parliaments, international institutions, and the United Nations. We have worked with Afghan men from different sectors. and Islamic scholars globally to foster solidarity and strategic approach. The past five years have been extraordinarily difficult for Afghan women, but we did not allow institutionalized discrimination to become normalized, and we will not. Dear colleagues, it's not that we do not appreciate the support provided to us, but it is too little and too slow in comparison to the crisis that we are dealing with. We need action, a sense of urgency, and the political will to change the situation and support Afghans who are working to achieve change on the ground inside the country and to provide a real alternative to the Taliban's oppression. I put forward five areas for discussion, debate, and most importantly, implementation before you. One, turn Afghan women's struggle into a global justice agenda. Afghan women's resistance is not only about our own rights. It's about global justice, universal human rights, and the integrity of the international system. That's why Afghan women are pursuing accountability through International Court of Justice, International Criminal Court, and the recognition and codification of gender apartheid as a crime against humanity. By codifying gender apartheid as a crime against humanity, we want to make sure that no woman or girl in any part of the world face what we are going through in Afghanistan today just because of our gender. Two, we urge international community to practice what you preach. This week, I have heard countless calls from member states, including regional and Islamic countries and the UN for women's rights and women's meaningful participation in Afghanistan. But the fact is, when it comes to Afghanistan, they are not putting these words into action themselves. We have seen this most clearly in the UN-led Doha process, where an invitation to the Taliban came at the price of Afghan women's participation. And what has the result been? A political process that is stalled and that has lost credibility in the eyes of ordinary Afghans? We need a credible, inclusive, Afghan-led and Afghan political process. And we need the international community to support us in crafting the roadmap towards that. If the international community insists on engaging the Taliban, so be it. But then it must also engage the women and men who are working to provide a democratic alternative. Three. Provide sustained, flexible, and meaningful resources to Afghan women-led organizations and movements, both inside Afghanistan and in exile. The funding mechanism must not only respond to immediate humanitarian crisis, it must also sustain leadership, organizing, documentation, advocacy, protection, and resilience of Afghan women. Four, respect our agency. We can speak for ourselves. What we need from the international community and anyone who has claimed to be our ally, not to speak for us, but to open the doors, provide platforms, and create space for Afghan women to speak for ourselves. Five, create a neutral convening space for Afghans. Afghan women and men, including democratic forces, need a safe space, a neutral space, where we can come together across political, geographic, and organizational differences. to exchange information, coordinate our advocacy, develop common strategies, and strengthen our collective action. Excellencies and dear colleagues, let me also spread some positive developments. This week, we had a number of productive meetings, including a meeting with Her Excellency, Deputy Secretary-General Amina Mohammed. These meetings gave many of us renewed optimism. We felt heard and understood. But most importantly, we felt a shared urgency to do something concrete to change the situation in Afghanistan. Let us move from statements to strategies, from promises to implementation, from fragmented efforts to coordinated actions, and from solidarity in words to solidarity in practice and action. We have to ensure the next five years is different from the past five years for Afghan women. Thank you.
Thank you, Ms. Nihan. I now invite Ambassador Isabelle Rome, France's Ambassador at Large for Human Rights and former Minister for Gender Equality. Ambassador Rome, please.

Ministers, Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, France extends its warmest thanks to Farah Ghia, Shamama, Women's Rights First, and the Afghan Charg d'Affaires for convening this meeting. As Minister for Gender Equality, and now as Ambassador for Human Rights, the support to Afghan women is one of my priorities. This year marks the fifth anniversary of the fall of Kabul to the hands of the Taliban. Five years on, the situation of the Afghan civilian population is deteriorating day by day before our very eyes, particularly that of women and girls, to such an extent that one wonders what basic rights remain to be taken away from them. I will not be too long, but I would like to recall France's strong commitment towards Afghan civilians, especially women and girls. France condemns the systematic violations of women and girls' rights by the Taliban. We do not compromise on the rights of Afghan girls and women. We firmly condemn the Taliban's vice and virtue law, which is a further illustration of the systematic assault on women and girls' rights. France ensures that references to women's rights are included in every resolution on Afghanistan. France has joined five other countries in referring the situation of women's and girls' rights in Afghanistan to the ICC. Afghan sisters who are fighters, Afghan civil society who have organized yourselves to find political and legal solutions through consultation, grounded in the reality of the Afghan people and their aspirations. As I like to say, to want to be free is to want others to be free. We want to be free. We want our Afghan sisters to be free. Thank you.
Thank you, Ambassador Rome. I now invite Her Excellency, Ambassador Beth Delancy, Australia's Deputy Permanent Representative to the United Nations in New York. Ambassador, you have the floor.

Thank you very much, and thank you for allowing us to join today, colleagues, friends. 15 August of this year marked a dark day. Five years on since the fall of Kabul and the Taliban's return to power, it is a grim milestone. The Taliban preside over one of the world's worst humanitarian crises. It is exacerbated by active efforts to dismantle development gains made during the period they were not in control, and their systematic exclusion of women from public space. Australia stands with the people of Afghanistan. On 29 January, Australia announced an additional $50 million in humanitarian support to the people of Afghanistan, with a strong focus on women and girls. This brings to over $310 million the total Australian humanitarian support provided to the people of Afghanistan since the fall of Kabul in 2021. Women and girls' human rights in Afghanistan, as in every country, are a global imperative. This is why Australia, together with Canada, the Netherlands and Germany, continues to pursue legal action against Afghanistan for violations of the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women. As our Foreign Minister has said, we will not accept the situation for women and girls in Afghanistan becoming a new normal. and Australia remains firmly committed to this initiative. We're also working with international partners to strengthen accountability for severe and systemic gender-based oppression. Australia is proud to be one of the first states to propose the crime of gender apartheid be recognised as a crime against humanity in the negotiations for a future treaty on crimes against humanity. The crime of gender apartheid is intended to capture the seriousness and full extent of the human rights violations perpetrated in state-designed systems of gender segregation and subordination. The Taliban's sustained assault on the human rights of women and girls has been deliberate and devastating, but it has not extinguished the courage, dignity and resilience of the Afghan people. Australia will continue to stand with them and with all those working for a more secure, inclusive and just future for Afghanistan. I thank you.

Thank you, Ambassador. And now we will go ahead and invite Ms. Kamila Azizi, co-founder of Shakhwama organization and an advocate for Afghan women's rights, justice and accountability. Ms. Azizi, please.

Thank you. Excellencies, distinguished delegates, colleagues, and friends, I have the honor of speaking on behalf of Shah Moma Organization, a woman-led organization dedicated to amplifying the voices of Afghan women and advancing justice, equality, and accountability. We meet at a critical moment for Afghanistan and for the international human rights system. For five years, Afghan women and girls have faced systematic restrictions on education, employment, freedom of movement, freedom of expression, participation in public life, and access to justice. These are not isolated violations. They form a system of discrimination and persecution affecting millions of Afghan women and girls. But Afghan women have refused to be silent. They have documented violations, continued to share knowledge, advocate, defend their communities, and speak for justice, often at extraordinary personal risk. Afghan women are not merely victims. They are rights holders, survivors, leaders, witnesses, and agents of change. Shah Moma's international advocacy has consistently emphasized that Afghan women's voices must remain at the center of international efforts for justice and accountability. Our June 2026 International Policy Conference in Geneva brought together governments, UN entities, international organizations, Afghan women leaders, and civil society to strengthen pathway toward justice and meaningful accountability. Today, I would like to highlight three important accountability pathways. First, the International Criminal Court provides a pathway to hold individuals accountable for serious international crimes, including the gender-based persecution of Afghan women and girls. Continued international support is essential to ensure that political power does not provide permanent immunity to those responsible. Second, The International Court of Justice provides a complementary pathway for the state's accountability. That denial of women's fundamental rights is not an internal matter. International law must continue to protect Afghan women and girls. Third, the Independent Investigative Mechanism for Afghanistan offers an important opportunity to move from documentation to accountability. It must be fully funded, operationalized, and supported by states. Its work must be gender-responsive and victim-centered. Afghan women must have a seat at the table, not a symbolic invitation, but meaningful participation in decision concerning justice, peace, accountability, and Afghanistan's future. We, therefore, call upon member states and international institutions to make five commitments. First, support and fund independent investigations and evidence preservation. Second, guarantee the meaningful participation of Afghan women, survivors, and women human rights defenders. Third, strengthen pathways to criminal accountability through the ICC, universal jurisdiction, and other legal avenues. Fourth, strengthen the international legal response to systematic gender-based persecution. Fifth, provide sustained support to Afghan women-led civil society organizations and human rights defenders documenting violations and supporting survivors. For survivors, justice means more than prosecution. It means truth. It means recognition, accountability, and the restoration of rights and dignity. As I conclude, I would like to emphasize one issue fundamental to every pathway toward justice for Afghan women and girls, documentation. Documentation is not simply about collecting facts. It is about preserving the truth, protecting survivors, and creating the evidence necessary for accountability. Every violations must be documented, preserved, and remembered. Let us move from documentation to investigations. from investigation to prosecution, and from prosecution to meaningful justice. Afghan women have carried the burden of documenting injustice for far too long. Now it is time for the international community to carry its responsibility to act. Nothing about Afghan women should be decided without Afghan women. for justice, for equality, for accountability, and for the future Afghanistan where every women and girls can live with dignity, freedom, equality, and hope. Thank you.

Thank you, Ms. Azizi. And thank you to all of our opening speakers. We now turn to our keynote statements, beginning with the voice from inside Afghanistan. We welcome our voice from inside of Afghanistan to begin now.

Excellencies, distinguished guests, ladies and gentlemen, thank you for giving me the opportunity to speak. I am joining you today from inside Afghanistan as an Afghan girl, and I want you to imagine something very simple. Imagine waking up one morning and being told that you can't go to school anymore. Not because you failed, not because you did something wrong, but simply because you are a girl. For Afghan girls, this is not something we have to imagine. This is our reality. We believed that education could never be taken away from us. We had dreams to learn, to go to university. to build our careers and to contribute to our country. Then everything changed. Our schools and universities were closed. And it felt like a piece of our future had been taken away. And now five years have passed since Taliban took control of Afghanistan. Five years in which the lives and freedoms of girls have changed dramatically. For girls, just like me, freedom has become smaller and smaller day by day. And in these five years, behind every restriction is a girl, a girl who simply wanted to live a peaceful life in Afghanistan. We Afghan girls, we are not asking for a special privilege. We are asking for a basic right. The right to learn, the right to work, the right to move freely, to dream, to choose their future. And when an Afghan girl loses access to education, it's not only one girl who loses. Afghanistan loses a generation of young women who could become doctors, teachers, scientists, leaders, and professionals across different fields. Afghanistan is not only a story of war. power to a political crisis. It's also a country of millions of young people with dreams. I am one of them. And I want the world to not forget us. But remembering us is not enough. We need opportunities. We need organizations to create meaningful pathways for Afghan girls to continue their education. Women's Rights First is one example of what that support can look like. By creating opportunities for Afghan girls to learn, develop digital skills, and become more independent, WRF has opened a window of hope for many Afghan girls who might have been left behind without a path forward. We need more opportunities like these. But we also need the word to open another door for us, student visas. For Afghan girls, whose schools and universities have been closed, studying abroad can be a lifeline. We need countries, including the United States, the United Kingdom, and our neighboring countries to keep pathways open for Afghan women and girls who want to study. And so I ask the world, if education inside Afghanistan is closed to us, why should the doors outside Afghanistan also be closed? If you cannot study at home, please do not close the doors that could allow us to study somewhere else. And this is what makes the situation even more painful. Instead of supporting Afghan students, Afghan girls, some doors around us are closing. Pakistan, for example, they have been expelling Afghan students from universities. including Afghan medical students in final years. For students, especially for girls, who have already lost the opportunity to study in Afghanistan, being forced to leave another place where they were continuing their education is truly devastating. We need the world to understand that there are not just policies or borders. Behind them are real students. real dreams, real futures. So please do not close the doors that could help us. Open them. Give Afghan girls opportunities to study. Give us scholarships, give us student visas, give us safe pathways to education. Because every Afghan girl deserves a chance to learn. And I speak here today not only for myself, but for thousands of Afghan girls who are waiting for a door to open. Girls who are ready to learn, who are ready to work hard, build their futures, if only they are given the opportunity. Five years have passed, but our dreams have not disappeared. We are still here. We are still learning. We are still dreaming. And we are still hoping. And at the end, I want to say, give us the chance to learn. And we will show what Afghan girls can achieve. Thank you so much.

Thank you so much for your voice and for sharing this important perspective with us. I now invite Mr. Richard Bennett, United Nations Special Rapporteur to the Situation of Afghanistan. Mr. Bennett, you have the floor.

Thank you very much, Ms. Nematullah. My thanks to the organizers, Farah Ghia, WRF, and Shamma Ma, and to Mr. Faik, the charge d'affaires. Let me begin by speaking directly to the girl who just addressed us all so powerfully. Your voice is probably the most important in this room. And I want to recommit to defending your human rights, the human rights of the thousands of girls that you referred to, and of all of the people of Afghanistan, especially those most marginalized, women and girls. ethnic, religious, and linguistically marginalized communities, LGBT community. The organizers provided some guiding questions, and I'm normally a rule breaker, but this time I followed the rules, so I'm going to respond to your questions. The first is, what's the international community achieved in five years? What progress has been made? Where have international efforts fallen short? And what lessons should guide the next phase of engagement? So five years after the Taliban seized power again, I think the international record is rather mixed. There have been some important achievements, depending on how achievement is measured. particularly on accountability and documentation, but if we measure success by whether the lives and rights of Afghans, especially women and girls, have improved, then we must acknowledge that the international community has fallen far short. There's been some important progress on accountability. And I give credit that the international community has largely refused to accept that the systematic dismantling of women's rights is simply an internal Afghan matter or something that can be justified by religion or culture. And the institutionalized system of discrimination, domination, and exclusion of women and girls is increasingly being examined through the lens of international crimes, including the crime against humanity of gender persecution. There have also been some other concrete developments. Gender apartheid has been mentioned already. Thank you, Australia. And this is an area where there, I believe, there is some momentum. Afghan women themselves are at the forefront of describing the Taliban system as gender apartheid. We must listen to them. And I too have increasingly described the situation facing women and girls as gender apartheid, an institutionalized system of gender-based discrimination, segregation, domination, and oppression. It should be used now, name it as a mobilizing factor, and also work towards codification. Don't have to wait. It's already been mentioned, the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for the Taliban's emir and the chief justice in relation to the crime against humanity of persecution on the grounds of gender. And also last year, or about a year ago, the Human Rights Council established the independent investigative mechanism. These have all been mentioned. These are significant developments. There's also an initiative by four countries using the CEDAW convention that may eventually go to the International Court of Justice. Five years ago, there was a legitimate fear that the enormous body of violations committed in Afghanistan would simply disappear in political negotiations. So today, at least, there is an emerging accountability architecture. And there has been continuing international documentation and scrutiny through my mandate, other UN mechanisms, Afghan civil society, and human rights organizations. And Afghan women themselves have played an extraordinary role in ensuring that what's happening inside the country is documented and remains on the international agenda. But these important achievements that they are cannot disguise the larger failure. There has not been a single reversal of any of the Taliban's discriminatory edicts. Every major restriction imposed on women and girls and others remains in place, and the system has become more institutionalized. I won't describe them, they've already been described today. So This forces us to ask a difficult question. What has international pressure actually changed on the ground? One weakness has been the absence of a sufficiently directive and coordinated international strategy. Different governments have pursued different priorities. humanitarian access, counter-terrorism, migration, regional stability, whatever. And the result too often has been engagement without leverage. At the same time, there's a temptation to normalize relations with the Taliban, which has grown, even though there has been no corresponding progress on fundamental rights. In fact, the evidence after five years points in the opposite direction. Restrictions have been codified step by step and enforcement mechanisms strengthened. Another major failure has been the declining attention to Afghanistan's humanitarian crisis. Humanitarian funding has contracted, has reduced. while poverty, food insecurity, and malnutrition remain severe. And millions of Afghans have been returned or forcibly returned from neighboring countries. These pressures disproportionately affect women and girls. So the lesson should not be that engagement has failed or that we should disengage. The question is, what kind of engagement? we should be pursued and what principles should govern engagement. I would emphasize a few lessons. First, engagement must be, as I mentioned, principled and coordinated. Governments should identify clear, measurable, and independently verifiable human rights benchmarks and coordinate their policies around them. And engagement should be used to press for change, not simply to manage relations with the Taliban. Second, engagement and normalization are different things. There are legitimate reasons to communicate with the Taliban about protection issues, about human rights obligations, about detainees, counterterrorism, humanitarian access. But diplomatic engagement should not translate into political legitimacy or normalization in the absence of meaningful changes in the Taliban's conduct. Third, Afghan women must be full, equal, and meaningful participants in decisions about the future of their own country, not merely subjects discussed at international meetings. Any international UN-led process concerning Afghanistan's future should include the full and meaningful participation of Afghan women. Fourth, accountability, as others have mentioned, must become operationalized. Establishing mechanisms is only the beginning. Fifth, we must not separate human rights from security and stability. Excluding half the population from education, employment, and public life has consequences far beyond women's rights. It affects Afghanistan's human capital, economy, healthcare system, institutions, and long-term stability. Finally, we mustn't lose sight of Afghan agency. One of the most important developments over the past five years has not come from governments or international institutions, it's come from Afghans themselves, women protesting despite the extraordinary risks, journalists continuing to report, human rights defenders documenting violations, educators finding ways to teach, and civil society actors continuing their work inside and outside Afghanistan. So the international community has made important progress in beginning to build an architecture of accountability, but it has not yet translated that progress into meaningful changes in the lives of Afghans. I think I'm out of time. There's just one kind of final thing I wanted to say about the lessons of the last five years, and that is that condemnation without consequences is not enough. The Taliban are constantly testing the limits of what the international community will tolerate. And after five years, they've learned that condemnation costs them little or nothing, and that red lines can be crossed without consequences. Every time we protest in words but continue to act as before, we send the same message: this is acceptable. We have to stop sending that message. Thank you very much. I will stop there. Thank you.

Thank you so much, Mr. Bennett, for your important perspective. It is now my pleasure to invite Her Excellency, Ambassador Janina, Permanent Representative of Albania to the UN. Ambassador, the floor is yours.

Thank you very much for giving me the floor, and also apologies from my side. My Prime Minister was delivering his national statement, and I couldn't join you before, but I'm really very happy to be representing my mission, Albania, as one of the co-sponsors of this important discussion. It is important in several dimensions. First, we are talking about five years, and I was thinking about what five years represent in each one's life. In the life of a nation, maybe it's a very short period of time. But in the life of one human being, it's a lot. In five years, a girl should have finished her academic cycle. So from one stage to another, we should have had a more educated girl and someone who had also the potential to contribute to the society. So that's the loss we are discussing about. We are discussing about the loss for Afghan girls, but also for Afghan society to be more inclusive, more developed. And when we talk about what we need to do, I think-- maybe I'm repeating myself. Nasser and Arjiss, you know, several times I've said that we have failed Afghan women and girls as an international community. We are talking a lot for five years. You have had also the occasions to come in the capital of my country, in Albania, in Tirana, to gather all the voices and also to maybe put aside that kind of prejudice that Afghan women voices is not together is a little bit divided. So you gave us a lesson, and you gave us the lesson of resilience, and also the lesson of coordination that is very much needed in these days. And here it comes, the most-- or the second important element, because we are talking about this, where the leaders one floor above us are talking about what the future should look like. Not everyone is mentioning what the future should look like for Afghan women. We know that it's not very clear, it's not very bright for the time being, but I believe that you have a mission, and together with us, we have a mission to speak up, to speak up about the rights of Afghan women and girls. We cannot be complacent with the situation as it is, and Afghan women and girls' cause should not be a crisis that is forgotten. It's there before our eyes. Maybe it's not very visible because we don't know exactly. We are hearing you, and we know that you are making really a big contribution to this cause, but most of you are not in Afghanistan. And when we need to hear from inside, we are lacking this kind of strength from there. So please speak up. I believe that together with my colleagues here, we have been committed more than once that we'll be by your side, but I think that coordination is another key word that we need to have in our minds. Together, we should know, and we are ready to give a space when the voice of Afghan women and girls is not only within the walls of the United Nations, but also outside to the capitals of member states. They should know, they should coordinate also among themselves. And as Mr. Bennett was telling to all of us, that we need also to put some conditions. We cannot go at business as usual. We cannot go and forgetting that politics is important, but there are rights, there are values, there are standards we need to stick to, to them. So on that regard, I believe that we have a lot to do together. I appreciate a lot that you are counting on Albanians' support. Thank you, Your Excellency. I now invite Ms. Alice Nelson, President and CEO of Vital Voices Global Partnership. Ms. Nelson, you have the floor.

Thank you. And thank you so very much to our incredible partners, wonderful allies that we have here who have really stood with Afghan women. Albania has been such an incredible friend, so thank you. Thank you for putting together this convening. You know, I was thinking about five years on, and as you say, five years in someone's life is a long time. And I think it's important that we don't just remember this day, but we know that we think about how these last five years, Afghan women, every single day inside the country, outside the country, have continued to fight. And they've done so with courage and conviction. And I think, I think all of us here think it is time that the world matched that courage and conviction that Afghan women have had. The world owes them more than remembrance. Five years on. We owe them action. And we need to match their courage and conviction. I'm not going to stand here today and or sit here today and talk and. cite statistics, you know, terrible statistics, horrific violations of women's human rights inside the country, because we're going to have a number of women from Afghanistan speak. And I think when they speak to those numbers, they will not just be speaking to numbers on a page and statistics. They will be speaking about their lives, stolen futures. Those that spoke, this young, brave woman who shared her story, And no one can speak to that reality with more accuracy, of course, than they can. What I want to speak about today is really what comes next and the partnership that it is going to take to get there. For 30 years, Vital Voices has been supporting and partnering with Afghan women. And I remember, this is 1996, long before technology was really a way to connect us and hear voices from women inside the country. But I remember hearing murmurings that women were setting up underground schools. Women were finding ways to care for other women, help them in childbirth and with health concerns underground. They were finding ways to connect. And then, of course, in 2001, when the Taliban was defeated, and everyone said, "Okay, well, what now for Afghan women?" And I remember that there were so many non-Afghans speaking about what it was that Afghan women wanted. And we knew, because we knew some of those women. We had gotten to know the work that they had done underground. We had a number of them come and worked with them and put them on TV to tell their own stories. One thing I have learned in these 30 years of working with Afghan women is that they are the strongest, the strongest, most courageous women on this planet. And often I am in awe that you continue to work with partners around the world who have failed you repeatedly. From 2001 until 2021, Vital Voices continued to support Afghan women through a number of different training programs with political leaders, women who were working to educate girls. Women were out on the front lines because they believed that the world had their back. So when the takeover came, for us, it was not a headline. No. We were not watching from the distance. We were hearing from women, calls, emails, calls for help, for support. And we knew immediately that we had to respond. We joined in coalition with Afghan and other American women, and we worked to evacuate extraordinary women leaders. I hate to say that we evacuated because I never want to make it sound as though somehow we were saviors. Certainly not. These were bold women who we had admired. They didn't want to leave. We knew that. No Afghan woman wanted to leave their country. Certainly not. They wanted to stay. They wanted to fight, but had no choice. And what we knew is if these courageous women, many of whom were on the Afghans infamous kill list did not get out of the country with their families, there would be no voice from the outside to remind people what is still going on in the inside. What has been astounding to me, and we did evacuate over 1,200 women leaders, 16 babies were born in those years, Thank you. A huge thank you to the government of Albania, who were extraordinary partners. It took four years to permanently resettle everyone who was evacuated, and Albania was an extraordinary host in those years. And please thank your prime minister. We are big fans. But what I think is totally astounding is that the women who evacuated, the women from Afghanistan, the women who have worked to rebuild their lives, whether in the United States or in Canada or other places around the world, they have never stopped pushing for our attention on what's going on inside the country. And I think about myself and I think, boy, if I had to leave my country with a backpack and run for my life, and just rebuild a livelihood, let alone a leadership path, would I have the strength to turn around and speak for others? And that is what these extraordinary Afghan women that are here today and many more have done. And it's been incredible to watch, astounding. From exile, they've done something remarkable, they've kept organizing, They lead a continued campaign against gender apartheid, which we're supporting, working alongside women still inside Afghanistan, women who teach in secret classrooms, who open pathways to remote work for young women, and who document human rights abuses at extraordinary personal risk. And we've not stopped, certainly, with just evacuating these leaders. and supporting them in those resettlement efforts. But we've tried to be there with them over these last five years. Now, I have to say it was very difficult because honestly, what is sort of sickening, no, it is sickening to me, is that everyone wanted to support the evacuation. But why is it that no one wants to come forth, not no one, but fraction of those people want to come forward and support these women now. To support their continued voice, to support these women still inside whose futures have been stolen. Why? It is time for the world to act. These are women who are boldly advocating inside and outside the country. They are pushing and advocating and training women inside the country as well around gender apartheid. Through these efforts, we've continued to support legal experts documenting human rights abuses, training young women to understand gender apartheid and build agency for global advocacy. That partnership between women in exile and women who have remained in Afghanistan is really a model I want to uplift today because it tells us exactly what the world now owes. It begins with the law. We call on every member state, and thank you very much to Australia, we call on every member state to formally support codifying gender apartheid as a crime against humanity in the treaty now under negotiation. Because until the law names what is happening in Afghanistan, accountability is going to remain out of reach. And we urge governments and civil society organizations, women leaders alike, to raise this consistently and by name in every bilateral and multilateral engagement, when the cameras are off, when the cameras are on, not as a footnote, but as a top priority. But naming the crime is only the start. We must continue to support Afghan women to empower them and equip them with the tools and resources they need to lead. That means standing behind networks with sustained support, whether it be supporting women who are educating girls in secret, supporting platforms that keep them safe, as schools and jobs have been, they have been barred from schools and jobs, and help organizations inside the country to continue their important work. Afghan women already have a voice. We know that. and a vision for their own future. What has been missing is not their leadership, it's sustained funding, protection, and political support to let that leadership reach its full scale. It also demands not that we see this clearly, it also and demands that we see this clearly and not in isolation. What is happening to women in Afghanistan is the most extreme form of oppression of a broader authoritarian playbook, one that is being studied and echoed by other regimes pushing back against women's rights around the world and undercutting the very way in which women lead. Governments and civil society organizations have a stake in how this moment is answered because a precedent is set right here. If we think somehow what's happening in Afghanistan doesn't affect what is happening in every other country around the world, we are sorely mistaken. But we know support alone is not enough. Afghan women must not just be present in shaping their country's future. They must hold real decision-making power in it. Thank you very much.

Thank you, Ms. Bradbury, and thank you for all of our keynote speakers today. Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. Thank you so much, Neelam John. The harder the Taliban try to erase us, the stronger we resist. They can silence a room, but they cannot silence a generation." I carry those words into this conversation because they hold something that edicts and the statistics cannot. And why are some states still hesitant to act, whether that's supporting the Sida case at the International Court of Justice, backing the International Criminal Court arrest warrants, or endorsing gender apartheid as a codified crime? Thomas Puthmajen. Thanks to our co-sponsors and also co-organizers, Sharmama and Farah Gil. I think this was a great opportunity for Afghan women to show their collaboration, their coordination, and their unified voice. And this is a point where the world can see that we have our collaboration, we have done our homework, and now it's time for the world to take the action and to support us in this fight. I also want to thank our fellow from inside Afghanistan. It's very late there, but she still stayed awake and contributed her voice. She was very keen to switch on her camera and to use her own name, but because of the security reason and her own safety and security, we couldn't make that possible, unfortunately. And I very much hope that one day every Afghan girl without any fear can freely speak. Before I start, today, Women's Rights First, in collaboration with Farah Gheer, Shahmama Rawadari, and 27 other Afghan women-led organizations and international organizations, issued a joint statement to mark the second anniversary of the SIDA invocation of Article 29 by the four member states, including Australian Ambassador who was here with us, Germany, Canada, and Netherland. and we very much hope that after two years, the member states would really take this case to the next procedural process, because it's been two years and we still don't see any tangible reason from this case. I think on your question, Sposma, there is this one important point that we need to be considerate of, is that all the accountability mechanisms, international accountability mechanisms that are trying to hold accountable for their violation, systemic violation of the rights of Afghan women and girls, whether that's the CEDAW case, which is still not officially filed with the ICJ. It has been invoked two years ago, and we are very much hoping to see the result. But the whole process is also a big advocacy point and also a point that can gather more support and attention to the situation of women and girls in Afghanistan. The mandate of the UN Special Rapporteur on human rights in Afghanistan the recently established double MA mechanism for Afghanistan, which is independent investigative mechanism for Afghanistan, the ICC proceedings, gender persecution and gender apartheid, they are all complementary mechanisms. They are all needed to work together. Sometimes I hear this from some of our friends and some of our experts that, If there is one mechanism working on Afghanistan, then there isn't a need for another mechanism. But as Special Rapporteur also highlighted in his statement, every mechanism has its own roles and responsibilities. The CEDAW process concerns state responsibility. It asks whether Afghanistan, as a state party to the CEDAW since 2003, is violating its treaty obligation. and what the states must do to hold its own member state accountable for violating its own treaties and the laws they have created. The ICC, by the contrast, concern individual criminal responsibility. On July 8, 2025, the ICC issued arrest warrants for Haibatullah Akhundzada, the Supreme Leader of the Taliban, and also Abdul Hakim Haqqani, after finding reasonable grounds to believe that they had ordered, induced, and solicited the crime against humanity of persecution on gender grounds against women and girls. And the third venue that has now been established, which is the independent investigative mechanism, is another complementary layer. What the investigative mechanism do is to collect, preserve, and analyze the evidence and prepare cases, case files for the national, regional, and international proceedings. One of the most critical point of the mechanism is that it also provokes the usage of universal jurisdiction, which is also another accountability mechanism that can be used for Afghanistan. Because previously, there wasn't ready cases to be used by the national courts and the national systems that have incorporated universal jurisdiction into their national laws. And now, civil society organizations, especially Afghan women-led organizations that are working on documentation, and that have the data can collaboratively work with the mechanism and they can hold all the perpetrators of human rights violations and war crime in Afghanistan wherever they are. So not only the Taliban, but also the violations that have been committed by the international forces in Afghanistan in the last 20 years, the violations that have been committed by the Taliban from 1996 to 2001, the violation that has been committed by the Mujahideen group before that, the violation that have been committed in Afghanistan since the Russian invasion in Afghanistan. So this mechanism will be working more comprehensively. And whenever there is data, there is evidence, that can be presented to the mechanism and that can be consolidated by the mechanism can be used to deliver the long due justice to the people of Afghanistan. And in describing the international community's role and responsibility toward using all these mechanisms and toward holding the Taliban accountable for what they are doing to Afghan women and girls, what we called is gender apartheid, is that I would ground it in what these institutions themselves have called for. When these institutions were established, they had set their own roles and responsibilities. And we are not asking them for anything extra. We are just asking them to implement what they were established for, to do their own job and their own work, in simple words, which is advancing the available accountability processes, cooperating with the members, with the ICC, the member states must support the ICC's investigation in Afghanistan because this is one of the very active venues that is still working on Afghanistan. I know there are a lot of political pressure on the ICC, but I think the case of Afghanistan should continue and the member states should support ICC's role in this case. As Kamila Jan also mentioned, there should be more support for the operationalization of the investigative mechanism so that it can work more collaboratively with Afghan civil society organizations and can also complement the work we are doing. And we are very much hopeful that the four member states that filed the ICJ case would not only take the case to the next procedural process, but will also provide more information to the public, in particular to Afghan women and girls. Unfortunately, there isn't enough information available at the moment to which we can follow through. And one of the main recommendations of today's statement was also focused on holding these states accountable for the case that they initiated two years ago, and it's still pending. On the issue of gender apartheid, I think It's been five years. The situation has been very clear. Afghan women are speaking, not only outside Afghanistan, but also inside Afghanistan, taking a very huge risk. So it is really the time for the international community to listen to us. Unfortunately, so many other political crises around the world is taking away the necessary attention to the situation of women and girls in Afghanistan. We really feel isolated. It's been five years that we are knocking on every door and we don't -- we still don't see any tangible result, unfortunately. We are very much thankful for the seven member states, including Australia and Iceland and other states that came forward and submitted a proposal for the codification of gender apartheid and we are hoping to see more coordinated action by the international community for the codification of gender apartheid. So I think it is also a political issue that some member states are hesitating to join this momentum for the codification of gender apartheid. There is also One of the other challenges is some legal vagueness, I would say, from our discussions with many experts. What we heard from them is that there are these other mechanisms that I mentioned, but there is also gender persecution already a crime against humanity for holding the Taliban accountable. So why don't we use gender persecution and why we are pushing for another overlapping legal term in the international law? But I think it is really critical for them to be very clear that It is the fact that gender persecution and gender apartheid describe overlapping harm, but they do not describe the same legal wrong. Persecution is defined around the intentional and severe deprivation of fundamental rights because of the identity of a group. The proposed definition of gender apartheid adds something more specific, an institutionalized regime of a systemic oppression and domination by one gender group over another together with the intention of maintaining that regime. That distinction is now expressly articulated in the formal state submission to the UN which was submitted by Iceland, Mexico, Timor-Leste's 2026 amendment proposal to the states. So this is the distinction and this is why we also need the gender apartheid to be codified, not only as a legal term but also because of the political support that codification of gender apartheid will bring to the women and girls in Afghanistan. But also what I always talk about and I have discussed this several times with my former colleague and special advocate Richard Bennett as well, is that unfortunately Afghanistan has always been a misogynistic state. And irrespective of the regime, women and girls have always suffered in Afghanistan. The codification of gender apartheid will bring that long due attention to the situation of women and girls, not only by the international community, but Afghans themselves. Afghans will realize that there is a huge gender problem in Afghanistan, and we need to pay more attention to it to solve it in a way that irrespective of whoever come to the regime after the Taliban or whoever is in the regime, they shouldn't be able to to violate the rights of women and girls and to erase a whole gender group, half of its society, from its public life. Thank you.

Thank you, Anifa John, for shedding light to the technical aspect of accountability mechanism meant to serve justice to Afghans, including women and girls. But if gender apartheid has one defining image, it is a girl turned away at the doorstep of school. Marjan Matin served as the Afghanistan's Deputy Minister of Education, leading national curriculum reform in teacher training, the very system now closed to the girls it was built to serve. Marjan, the education ban is one of the clearest tools of gender apartheid in Afghanistan. What concrete support, be it diplomatic, financial, and technical, does the international community still need to provide to sustain and scale education alternatives? And how do we challenge the narrative that treats this as a cultural issue rather than a deliberate system of exclusion?

Thank you so much, Ms. Bushma, and thank you for the co-organizers and also the co-sponsors of today's side event, and also for giving me the opportunity to speak here. If we understand gender apartheid as a system that excludes women and girls from society, the education ban is one of the ways that that system is sustained. It does more than keep girls and women out of the classroom. It limits their qualifications, it limits their independence, and it also limits their choices that they can have as an adult. It reduces the number of women who can teach and also who can care for the future Afghan generation. The response must work on two tracks. First, as we all are already doing, keep the girls and women learning. And second, restore their right to formal education as part of a wider effort to end Afghan women's exclusion. The international community should provide sustained funding, as Tony mentioned, for community-based education, accelerated learning, scholarships, literacy programs, and most importantly, expand support to the teachers. I think teachers play a very important role in the society, especially for those women who have lost their jobs as teachers. It should fund Afghan organizations that know their communities very well and can respond swiftly and quickly when conditions change and if conditions change. Online lessons cannot reach every girl, so technical support must also include offline materials. We very well know that giving the girls and women access to physical books is not feasible, not just financially, but also security-wise, but providing them the softwares and the technical tools to access those Books and curriculum offline is very important. Of course, train those teachers who have lost their jobs and who still continue to go and work and also provide safe learning spaces. We must be honest here and acknowledge the limits of these alternative learnings. A girl may study for years outside of a formal space and school. but she will still be unable to sit an exam, to enter university, or to qualify for a profession. We need ways for girls to demonstrate what they have learned. And here, I want to emphasize that we have to find mechanisms and ways that we can carry out learning assessments for those who have been informally learning. Alternative learning, therefore, must never become acceptable, and it should not also be the reason to normalize the ban on education. The international community, we've all seen that they have condemned the ban many times with public statements, but if those are considered as measures and if those measures have not brought any change in a woman's or girl's life on the ground, then there needs to be a drastic change of course in how international community wants to deal with the situation on the ground. Governments need a common plan for what happens after each statement when they do that. They should set public benchmarks, and those are not difficult to set forward or to define. Simple, girls returning to secondary school. It's not like a rocket science. Women return to university and return to their work, return to health training, and women teachers being allowed to work. Afghan women educators and also civil society organizations are very good partners for the international community to help them assess how each of these measures are taking progress on the ground and how it's impacting the practices. Governments also have leverages, other leverages, and one of them can be, they can make these benchmarks central since we already know that the governments are holding meetings with the Taliban. So why not just make these benchmarks central to meetings with those officials, with the Taliban officials, and also to decisions about high-level visits or expanded diplomatic engagement as we see being normalized. Expand the UN travel ban instead of giving them concessions on those travel bans and enforce them as part of the measure to put pressure. And governments should also support efforts to document abuses and violations of human rights and also help Afghans pursue accountability, especially those who are bearing the brunt of these draconic policies on the ground. And the pressure must be coordinated, of course. We heard a lot about coordination, but the coordination amongst these governments is very key. If one government raises education as part of the agenda in the meeting, while another one offers political access without conditions. So these measures are never going to take-- never going to turn to reality. And as Mr. Bennett mentioned, I think it will just normalize that Taliban can cross the red lines, and it's just going to be a normal norm. education and, and this does not mean that education and humanitarian funding should not reach the communities, but the aim here is to put pressure on those responsible for the ban without adding any further to the hardship that Afghan women and girls are already bearing and the families that they are being impacted. There is also, I want to also emphasize that there is, there's a long-term peace and security dimension here as well. And I want to be precise here that a girl denied education might not be seen as a security threat, but the risk lies in what Afghanistan loses when girls cannot become teachers, nurses, doctors, or can earn a living. A school without women teachers will struggle to educate the next generation of Afghans, a clinic without trained women health workers will struggle to care for mothers and children in the future, and they are already now. Maternity. Mortality. Mortality is increasing. These losses build over time and weaken the services and institutions that will keep Afghanistan stable. Therefore, impacting the stability in the region and the world as well. UNICEF I know we all are very familiar with these estimates and numbers, but I just want to mention it because it's important. UNICEF estimates that restrictions on girls' education and women's employment already cost Afghanistan at least $84 million in lost economic output each year. The country could lose more than 25,000 teachers and health workers by 2030 if the restrictions continue. These are consequences for families today, and for Afghanistan's ability to recover in the future as well. And finally, I would also like to, as many of you have echoed in your speeches and remarks, the claim that girls' education is a cultural issue. Afghan women, parents, teachers, and community organizations continue to find ways to keep girls learning. And the society that are being governed under the Taliban is the very same society that was thriving before 2021. And it's the same society that had school shuras who would extend their community support to the schools, whether it was infrastructure, whether it was advocating amongst local communities to let families, to mobilize families to send their girls and women to become teachers and also to provide those access. It's the same, it's the very same society, yes, being governed by the Taliban, but it's the very same society that was there thriving before the fall in 2021. So the international community should really match that very determination that Afghan families and especially Afghan women have by protecting the learning opportunities, mechanisms, and of course, demanding full access to education and work, and refusing to treat women's exclusion as normal. Education is part of the infrastructure of peace. Keeping it alive today protects Afghan girls' rights and helps preserve the people and institutions of Afghanistan will need tomorrow, therefore also contributing to a more peaceful region and the world in the future. Happy to answer any questions.

Thank you, Marjan. Counting down the days to have you redesign a more progressive national curriculum this time. human rights at its core, because if a generation of girl is shut out of human rights education, the consequences reach far into Afghanistan's future. Few keep that future in view as deliberately as Sana Amini, who works to ensure Afghan women inside the country, in exile, and in the next generation have a genuine voice in the decisions that shape their lives. Excellencies, distinguished representative, colleagues, and dear friends, I am happy to -- I am here today. What concerns me most is that an entire generation of Afghan women is losing the years of their education, opportunity, and freedom. Girls being denied education has become normalized. It has been about five years that they cannot go to school, they cannot go to university, or they cannot go to their jobs. If it continues, the poverty rate, forced marriages, unemployment will increase more and more. Think of a girl who was in sixth grade in 2021, who had dream to graduate from high school, or a girl who wanted to start college, or a girl who wanted to finish college and fulfill their dreams, but their dream just remain as a dream. If it continues, Afghanistan could lose a generation of educated women, teachers, doctors, engineers, scientists, politicians, future leaders. One educated generation leads to another. This restriction is not part of our culture or lack of ambition. Afghan women are the more talented and ambitious women, but they didn't had the opportunity to continue it. And also, Afghan women's rights is not just about Afghan women. It is human rights. It is universal rights. Education is not something to be given to us. It is our right, and it should be our right. Being here today is deeply personal to me. Afghanistan is not simply as a subject of discussion. It is my home. It's where I grew up, went to school, and dream about my future. Their education and their university remain closed to them. Their freedom has been restricted, and decision about their own future have been taken out of their hands. So when I speak about Afghan women today, I'm not speaking about the struggle that is distant from me. I lived part of it. The difference is that I was given a way to move forward, while so many Afghan women and girls are still waiting for theirs. My story is only one among millions. And it is why Afghan women must have the meaningful voice in decision that shape their lives and their future. For years, we have been consulted, we have been invited to conferences, we have shared our experience, but there is an important question we must ask. After Afghan women are consulted, who actually make the decision? Being invited to speak is not the same having seat in decision-making table. Consultation ask Afghan women, what do you think?
